core_principles: Fundamental movement competency is essential for physical activity participation and reducing injury risk.
The squat movement pattern is a critical fundamental movement necessary to improve sport performance, reduce injury risk, and support lifelong physical activity.
Competence in fundamental movements must be developed as an essential component of preparatory training before engaging in vigorous physical activity and organized, competitive sport.
Fundamental movement patterns (such as running, throwing, lunging, and squatting) have direct biomechanical and neuromuscular implications for successful performance in dynamic sports tasks.
Establish proficiency in the bodyweight back squat before progressing to externally loaded variations or plyometric training.
Begin in a standing position with feet flat on the floor, knees and hips in a neutral, extended position, and the spine upright preserving its natural curves.
Descend by flexing the hips, knees, and ankles until the top of the thigh is at least parallel with the ground and the hip joint is level with or slightly below the knee joint.
Ascend via triple extension of the hips, knees, and ankles to return to the starting position.
Engage the posterior torso muscles, specifically the erector spinae, isometrically to maintain an upright posture throughout the movement.
Utilize the squat as a closed kinetic chain exercise in rehabilitation to limit excessive strain on the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL).
common_mistakes: Progressing to loaded squats or plyometrics before mastering the bodyweight squat technique.

core_principles: Stiffen the torso by creating tension in the abdominal wall using both posterior torso muscles and anterior/lateral abdominal muscles.
Inhale to approximately 80% of maximal inhalation and hold the breath (Valsalva maneuver) before starting the descent to increase intra-abdominal pressure and stabilize the spine.
Use the Valsalva maneuver to establish proximal stiffness, which enhances force output and velocity in the limbs.

Assess the back squat using the Back Squat Assessment (BSA) across three domains: upper body (head, neck, torso), lower body (hips, knees, ankles), and movement mechanics (timing, coordination, recruitment).
Perform 10 continuous back squat repetitions for a complete assessment, analyzing movement from anterior, posterior, and lateral perspectives.
Standardize the assessment setup using a lightweight cylindrical dowel held with a pronated grip slightly wider than shoulder-width, resting on the contracted upper back musculature.
common_mistakes: Failing to create sufficient abdominal wall tension to stiffen the torso.
Inadequate breath control or failing to utilize the Valsalva maneuver to stabilize the spine under compressive loads.
Failing to maintain proper technique across 2 or more repetitions during the 10-repetition assessment.
specific_findings: Inhale approximately 80% of maximal inhalation and hold their breath to increase intra-abdominal pressure.
The Back Squat Assessment (BSA) screening tool utilizes ten criteria to be scored, subcategorized into 3 comprehensive domains: upper body, lower body, and movement mechanics.
To initiate the assessment, the athlete should be asked to perform 10 continuous back squat repetitions.
A deficit should be marked if the individual fails to demonstrate the desired technique of a criterion to perfection during 2 or more repetitions.
A lightweight cylindrical dowel (wooden, metal, or plastic; approximately 1¼ $ 3 36$ long) is recommended to be used to set-up the athlete.

core_principles: Grip the dowel with a pronated grip slightly greater than shoulder-width apart.
Position the dowel across the posterior deltoids, just below C7 of the cervical spine.
Rest the dowel comfortably on the contracted upper back musculature.
Hold forearms parallel to the torso.
Keep the back straight and un-flexed throughout the movement.
Instruct the athlete to 'bend the bar' (pulling it into the trapezius) to engage the back extensors, shoulder retractors, and latissimus to stiffen the torso.
If a dowel is unavailable, mimic holding one with open palms under the ears while retracting the scapulae.
Assume an initial stance with heels approximately shoulder-width apart and toes pointing forward or slightly outward.
Hold the dowel in a back squat position with forearms parallel to the torso and upper back musculature contracted.
Squat down until the top of the thighs are at least parallel to the ground, then return to the starting position.
Perform 10 continuous repetitions at a consistent, moderate pace for the Back Squat Assessment (BSA).
Ensure the neck demonstrates adequate pain-free physiological range of motion (flexion, extension, rotation, and side bending) before training.
common_mistakes: Using extreme stance widths and extreme foot positions (tibial rotation) during initial instruction.
Adopting an excessively wide stance, which increases knee joint compressive forces.
Adopting an excessively narrow stance, which increases forward knee translation and anterior shear forces.
Allowing extreme tibial rotation in a closed-chain movement, which increases stress on static knee structures.
specific_findings: A wide stance may increase patellofemoral and tibiofemoral compressive forces in the knee joint by up to 15% during descent.
Initial stance toes should point forward or slightly outward by no more than 108 [10 degrees].
Athletes should not exceed 30 8 [30 degrees] of internal ankle rotation or 80 8 [80 degrees] of external rotation to maximize stability and promote normal patella tracking.

core_principles: Maintain the head and neck in neutral alignment to slight extension with the torso to provide a strong, balanced set-up.
Keep the neck held in line to the plane of the torso.
Direct the gaze either straight ahead or slightly upward.
Use a slightly upward gaze during ascent to help lead with the head and chest rather than raising the hips first, and to prevent excessive forward trunk flexion.
Assess head position (chin position, anterior/posterior tilt) from the lateral perspective, and gaze direction from the anterior perspective.
Ensure the neck is perpendicular to the line of the shoulders with no lateral tilt from the posterior perspective.
common_mistakes: Moving the head too far forward, backward, or laterally during the squat.
Excessive tilting of the head backward into extreme cervical hyperextension, which can be dangerous under heavy resistance and may compensate for a lack of thoracic extension.
Excessive cervical flexion, which can lead to compensatory lumbar spine extension and increased lumbar compression forces.
Cervical hyperflexion (looking too far downward), which can cause a significant increase in hip and trunk flexion.

core_principles: Maintain a neutral head and neck position throughout the entire squat movement.
Disassociate gaze from head position, allowing a slightly upward gaze without deviating the head from a neutral alignment.
Keep the thoracic spine slightly extended and held rigid to sustain a stable, upright posture.
Direct the chest outward and upward to bring the torso angle to a more vertical position.
Retract and depress the scapulae while maintaining relative external rotation of the glenohumeral joint.
Keep forearms parallel to the spine and shoulders retracted to maximize spinal stability from supporting back muscles.
common_mistakes: Directing the gaze too far downward, which increases hip and trunk flexion.
Deviating the head and neck from a neutral position due to neck muscle weakness, poor postural awareness, or limited mobility.
Failing to keep the chest upward, causing it to point toward the ground.
Flexing or excessively extending the thoracic spine during the lift.
Allowing the scapulae to relax or protract, resulting in forward-rolled shoulders.
specific_findings: A downward gaze has been shown to increase hip flexion and potentially trunk flexion in comparison with an upward gaze, placing increased torque on the vertebral column (Citations 2, 6, 43).

Positioning the forearms parallel to the spine with retracted shoulders allows major supporting back muscles (latissimus dorsi, erector spinae, trapezius, rhomboids) to contribute maximally to spinal stability (Citation 28).

A propensity for forward rolled shoulders during the back squat may be due to lifestyle-induced postural weaknesses such as upper crossed syndrome, which results from consistently internally rotated shoulders leading to excessively shortened or tight pectorals.
Any flexion or excessive extension of the thoracic spine, either constantly or sporadically, is indicative of biomechanical compensatory strategies (Citation 3).

core_principles: Maintain a stiffened torso with a neutral, lordotic lumbar position throughout the entire squat movement to preserve the spine's load-bearing capacity.
Keep the trunk as upright as possible during the squat to minimize lumbar shear forces associated with forward lean.
Preactivate the stabilizers of the trunk and hip (including lower back musculature, obliques, lumbar paraspinals, quadratus lumborum, and abdominals) to counterbalance unwanted motion.
Hold the abdomen upward and rigid to promote spinal stability.
Ensure the line of the trunk remains parallel to the line of the tibias when viewed from the lateral perspective.
Maintain scapular retraction and an open chest to avoid thoracic position deficits.
common_mistakes: Allowing the chest to drop or failing to retract the scapulae during the squat.
Difficulty dissociating the thoracic position from the lower trunk position.
Inability to maintain a chest-up position due to weakness in the erector spinae, trapezius, and rhomboids.
Excessive tightness in the chest (potentially from upper crossed syndrome) hindering the ability to open the chest.
Failure to stiffen the lower back musculature, allowing the trunk to collapse downward into excessive flexion.
Wavering or displacement of the trunk during the execution of the squat.

core_principles: Maintain a neutral, slightly lordotic spine posture throughout the squat to avoid excessive pressure on the lower back.
Stiffen the back musculature (thoracic and lumbar paraspinals) and parascapular musculature to maintain retracted and depressed scapulae.
Maintain tension in the thoracolumbar fascia through the integration of the posterior chain and back musculature.
Ensure the trunk angle remains parallel with the tibial angle during the squat.
Use a dowel-only squat to at least parallel to assess pelvic tilt and movement patterns without heavy external resistance.
common_mistakes: Excessive trunk flexion (forward lean) during the squat.
Rounding of the spine (kyphosis) due to relaxed back musculature and spinal flexion.
Restricting knee translation, which can increase anterior forward lean of the trunk.
Tilting the head forward, which can place excessive pressure on the lower back.
Flexing the spine prematurely before reaching deep hip flexion.
Excessive anterior or posterior pelvic tilt.
specific_findings: Flexing at the spine before 120 degrees of hip flexion when squatting may indicate restriction in the posterior fibers of the iliotibial band or lack of lumbar control.

core_principles: Maintain a neutral pelvic tilt during the squat to increase erector spinae and oblique muscle activity, providing optimal spinal support.
Recruit the gluteal muscles properly to prevent the quadriceps from bearing excessive load, reducing the risk of muscle imbalance and injury.
Utilize the hamstrings to control hip flexion during the descent and to extend the hips during the ascent phase.
Engage hip abductors (gluteus medius and minimus) to stabilize the femurs and prevent the knees and hips from rotating inward during descent.
Maintain square, stable hips with minimal mediolateral movement, ensuring the line of the hips is parallel to the ground in the frontal plane.
Determine squat depth based on the position of the hips, keeping femur position symmetrical throughout the movement.
common_mistakes: Asymmetrical hip movement, such as leaning, dropping, or twisting to one side.
Internal rotation of the femurs during descent, which may be caused by tight hip adductors.
Compensatory increased trunk flexion caused by a lack of hip mobility.
The dowel dropping down to one side during the squat.

core_principles: Knees should track directly over the toes throughout the squat motion, maintaining a neutral frontal plane knee position.
The foot should be positioned to create a perfect in-line hinge with knee motion, avoiding medial or lateral knee displacement.
Closed kinetic chain exercises like the back squat can support rehabilitation after ligament reconstruction surgery.
Allowing natural anterior tibial translation (knees moving past toes) is acceptable, as restricting it artificially increases forward trunk lean and hip/spine forces.
Keep feet firmly planted on the floor throughout the movement.
common_mistakes: Knee valgus (medial or knock-kneed movement) during the squat, often caused by weak hip abductors/external rotators, overactive hip adductors, or restricted ankle dorsiflexion.
Knee varus (outward knee movement), which can occur as a compensatory strategy in athletes with flat feet.
Consciously restricting forward knee travel past the toes, which forces excessive forward trunk lean and increases injury risk at the hip and spine.
Active valgus, where hip adduction and knee abduction occur due to suboptimal active neuromuscular patterns.
specific_findings: The lateral aspect of the knee should not cross the vertical plane of the medial malleolus when assessing for medial displacement.
The medial aspect of the knee should not cross the vertical plane of the lateral malleolus.
Forces on the cruciate ligaments of the knee decrease at high flexion angles (43).
Conscious effort to restrict forward translation has been shown to increase forward trunk lean, resulting in significantly greater forces at the hip and spine (16, 23).
Tibiofemoral and patellofemoral compression increases with increasing knee angle, initiating a protective co-contraction between the quadriceps and hamstrings (43).

core_principles: Initiate the squat descent by breaking the hips back.
Attempt to match the tibia angle in parallel with an upright trunk while keeping heels on the ground.
Allow knees to move freely in accordance with hip range-of-motion, noting that tibial translation varies based on individual torso and leg length ratios.
Maintain a flat and stable foot position, keeping the entire foot on the ground throughout the entire squat motion.
Shift the center of pressure in the foot from the mid-foot during initial stance toward the heel and lateral foot during the descent phase.
common_mistakes: Excessive anterior translation of the knees over the toes.
Overly restricted tibial translation during the squat, which forces an excessive anterior lean of the torso.
Allowing heels to lift off the ground.
Shifting load excessively to the knees instead of the gluteals/rear due to weak gluteal muscles.
Excessive tibial progression angle caused by weakness in the calf, soleus, hamstrings, or quadriceps dominance.
Restricted tibial progression due to tight gastrocnemius, soleus, talocrural joint restrictions, or hip and foot mobility deficits.
specific_findings: Overly restricted tibial translation during the squat increases anterior lean of the torso, which accompanies increases in hip torque and lumbar shear forces (16).
Excessive anterior translation of the knees over the toes is purported to increase shearing forces on the knee and greater knee extensor torque (30).
The suggested center of pressure in the foot moves from the mid-foot during initial stance toward the heel and lateral foot ('L' foot loading position) during the descent phase of the squat.

core_principles: Emphasize body weight through the heel and lateral foot during descent while keeping toes on the ground to ensure balance.
Placing weight toward the back of the foot facilitates desired hip motion strategies during the entire squat phase.
Placing weight toward the lateral aspect of the foot encourages improved recruitment of the gluteal muscles.
Keep the medial side of the foot on the ground to promote balance and stability, ensuring the calcaneus does not evert relative to the lower leg.
Initiate the descent by breaking at the hips (hip hinging) while maintaining a rigid, upright trunk.
Reach back as if sitting in a chair that is slightly too far away, keeping the rear as far away from the ankles as possible.
Maintain a constant vertical distance between the shoulders and hips throughout the descent.
Transfer and support body weight using the posterior chain musculature (hamstrings and gluteals) rather than placing it anteriorly on the knees.
common_mistakes: Pronation or supination of the feet (rolling feet inward or outward).
Lifting heels or toes off the ground during the squat.
Ankle inversion or eversion.
Excessively rapid or unsteady movement during descent.
Failing to maintain constant speed and control during the eccentric phase.
Placing load down on the anterior aspect of the knees rather than back on the hips during descent.
specific_findings: The athlete should move at a controlled tempo with no less than 2:1 (descent:ascent) up to a 4:1 ratio in regard to velocity of the eccentric movement compared with the concentric ascent phase.
Allowing the heels to rise off the ground has been observed to create compensatory torques about the ankles, knees, hips, and lumbar spine (3).

A lack of strength in the medial gastrocnemius, tibialis anterior, and/or tibialis posterior decreases the athlete's ability to control knee valgus and foot pronation motions and may contribute to excessive medial knee displacement and dynamic valgus (1).

core_principles: Master controlled descent strategies to mitigate the risk of training-induced injuries.
Maintain sufficient posterior chain (hamstrings and gluteals) strength to retain control during the later phases of the descent.
Avoid rapid, high-velocity eccentric movements if the muscles are forced to stretch too quickly.
common_mistakes: Losing descent control toward the later phases of the movement.
Favoring a knee-loading strategy, which increases forces on the anterior knee and decreases posterior chain recruitment.
Allowing muscles to stretch too greatly in a short amount of time during intense squat variations.

core_principles: Use a hip-hinge strategy rather than a knee-loading strategy during the descent.
Maintain eccentric control during the descent, aiming for a controlled tempo rather than dropping into the apex.
Achieve full depth with the tops of the thighs at least parallel to the ground.
At the bottom of the squat, keep the hips back, tibias vertical, and feet flat on the ground.
Drive the ascent primarily through the hips, keeping weight on the heels and lateral sides of the feet.
Ensure the shoulders and hips rise at the same pace during ascent, keeping the torso angle relatively constant.
Keep the back rigid and tight with the lumbar spine in a neutral to slightly extended position.
Exhale only after the ascent has been fully completed.
common_mistakes: Knee-loading strategy during descent, characterized by excessive trunk flexion, excessive tibial progression, or heels lifting.
Dropping too quickly into the bottom of the squat due to lack of eccentric control.
Squatting too shallow, failing to bring the thighs at least parallel to the ground.
Hips rising faster than the shoulders during the early ascent, which increases trunk flexion and stress on the lower back.
Allowing the knees to drift too far back during ascent, forcing a forward torso lean to maintain balance.
Allowing the knees to drift too far forward during ascent, shifting weight onto the toes and disrupting hip drive.
specific_findings: Descent timing is expected to maintain a 2:1 ratio in relation to ascent.
At the proper depth, the femurs are positioned slightly past parallel to the ground.

core_principles: During the squat ascent, the hips and shoulders should rise at the same rate, keeping the vertical distance between them constant.
Anatomical variations, particularly hip joint structure and the ratio of torso length to leg length, dictate individual squat depth and mechanics.
A deeper hip joint socket increases standing stability but physically restricts deep hip flexion, meaning deep squats may cause labrum or joint capsule pinching for some individuals.
Bony restrictions in the hip joint cannot be overcome or corrected by stretching or mobility work.
Assessment of hip anatomy limitations can begin with the individual kneeling on their hands and knees.
common_mistakes: Hips rising too quickly in relation to the shoulders during the ascent.
Concentric weakness in the posterior chain and hip extensors during the ascent.
Insufficient thoracic spine and hip flexor mobility.
Attempting to force a deep squat past bony anatomical restrictions, risking impingement of the hip joint labrum and capsule.
specific_findings: The text references the '10 BSA criteria' (Bodyweight Squat Assessment) as the ideal standard for athlete positioning.
A deeper hip joint socket creates a physical bony restriction that prevents deep femur flexion without pinching the hip joint labrum and joint capsule.

core_principles: Use the pelvic rock test to determine the optimal width for the feet and knees when squatting and to quantify deep squatting ability without losing neutral spine curvature.
Knee travel relative to the toes is a function of the individual's leg length to torso length ratio.
Athletes with longer legs relative to their torso should squat with their hips further back to balance knee and hip loads.
Athletes with a longer torso relative to leg length should squat with more emphasis on knee motion, keeping the shin parallel to the torso to equally share hip and knee loads.
Proficiency with the unloaded back squat is a mandatory prerequisite before progressing to heavy resistance squat training or advanced variations like depth jump plyometrics.
Do not increase squat intensity or resistance unless the athlete can consistently demonstrate proper form.
common_mistakes: Allowing the neutral spine curvature to flex during a deep squat.
Using compensatory movement strategies due to poor mechanics, which can propagate into sport competition and heighten injury risk.
Increasing exercise intensity or resistance before mastering the basic unloaded back squat movement pattern.
specific_findings: The pelvic rock test: knees are initially placed together, the pelvis is rocked back toward the heels, and the test stops when the neutral spine curvature begins to flex.
A 7-foot tall basketball center usually has longer legs than torso, such that the knees travel way ahead of the toes.
The length of the femur creates a long lever and a high patellar tendon load.
An individual with a longer torso to leg length ratio squats with more emphasis on knee motion, and the shin remains parallel to the torso, equally sharing hip and knee loads.

core_principles: Identification and correction of functional deficits using the bodyweight squat can improve performance and reduce injury risk in young athletes.
Utilizing the bodyweight squat as an assessment tool promotes long-term physical well-being and athletic career success.
common_mistakes: Excessive medial knee displacement

core_principles: Incorporate neuromuscular training to improve athletic performance and lower-extremity biomechanics, particularly in female athletes.
Utilize neuromuscular training strategies to help mitigate the risk of ACL injuries.
Integrate cognitive developmental considerations when designing and implementing training programs for youth.
specific_findings: Neuromuscular training improves performance and lower-extremity biomechanics in female athletes (Myer GD, Ford KR, Palumbo JP, and Hewett TE. J Strength Cond Res 19: 51–60, 2005).
